title: Uncertainty-Aware Gaussian Map for Vision-Language Navigation
one_liner: The agent builds a map of 3D Gaussian shapes and explicitly tracks three types of measurement doubt (geometric, semantic, appearance) to navigate reliably when instructions are ambiguous.
lead: When a robot follows natural language instructions to navigate a building, it faces uncertainty at every step: the walls might be unclear in the image, the words might mean different things in that space, or the colors might shift with lighting. Rather than ignoring this doubt, this paper makes the agent reason about it explicitly. The agent constructs a map made of 3D Gaussian primitives (smooth, probabilistic blob shapes in space) and marks which parts of the map are unreliable, using that doubt to make safer navigation decisions.

problem.h2: The agent does not know what it does not know
paras: A robot navigates by reading instructions ("go forward until the blue door, turn left") and looking at camera images of the building. But reality is messy: the image might show a shadowy corner where walls are hard to see; the word 'kitchen' might be true but ambiguous if two similar rooms appear; or the color is different under different lights. A naive agent simply chooses the best-guess next move anyway, even when the evidence is weak. It confidently says 'go left' when it is actually guessing.

When evidence is weak, confident guesses lead to failures. The agent bumps into walls it could not see clearly, or ends up in the wrong room because multiple places matched the description equally well. A better approach would be: measure the doubt and use it to steer clear of risky moves. This works because when you know an area is unreliable, you can avoid it instead of blundering through and failing.

callout.html: The agent builds a map that explicitly marks where it is uncertain, so it can navigate cautiously when the evidence is weak.

steps.text: Create a 3D map using Gaussian blob shapes from the robot's panoramic view.
Jiggle each blob's position and size slightly; see how much that changes what the map looks like.
Perturb the meaning labels on each blob to find places where multiple interpretations are equally likely.
Use Fisher Information (a metric of how sensitive predictions are to small changes) to find where colors are unreliable.

steps.b: Make decisions with the doubt map
steps.text: When choosing the next move, avoid high-uncertainty regions; prefer clear evidence over weak guesses.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the agent's internal map
paras: Instead of building a single best-guess map, the agent now builds a map that stores doubt explicitly at every location. Each 3D Gaussian blob carries not just its position and meaning, but also a reliability score measuring how much the agent trusts that blob.
object.object: the Semantic Gaussian Map (now with uncertainty)

hidden.name: per-location uncertainty
paras: Uncertainty is not just a feeling; it is a measurable quantity. At each point in the map, the agent can ask: 'If I nudge the wall position slightly, does my prediction change a lot?' If yes, that spot is unreliable. If no, the agent has strong evidence. The paper measures this by perturbing Gaussian position and scale, observing how much the predictions shift, and recording that sensitivity as a number.

The paper actually estimates THREE separate uncertainties: geometric (does the wall position shift the answer?), semantic (do different object labels fit equally?), and appearance (do lighting changes throw off color matching?). These are baked into the map as a 3D Value Map, so the navigation system can reason about doubt in real time.

heat.caption: Darker means less reliable. A wall in shadow (App-Shadow) is less certain than a wall in clear light.

reads.html: The map stores a doubt score at every blob. High doubt means 'the walls might be in the wrong place, the label might be wrong, or the color might fool us.' Low doubt means 'we have strong evidence this spot is what we think.'

Geometric uncertainty is estimated via variational perturbations of Gaussian position and scale; semantic uncertainty via perturbations of semantic attributes; appearance uncertainty via Fisher Information of rendered observations with respect to Gaussian-level variations.

mechanism.h2: Why measuring doubt makes the navigation work better
paras: A robot following instructions must make a choice at each step: go forward, turn left, turn right, or stop? The naive way is to pick the move that looks most likely given the current image. But when the image is ambiguous, all moves might look equally plausible. The robot does not know it is guessing.

This paper changes that by building a map of uncertainty first. When the robot considers a move, it checks: does this move take me through a high-uncertainty region? If yes, the move is risky—maybe there is a wall I could not see clearly, or maybe I misunderstood the room label. Instead, the robot can prefer moves that go through certain regions, or choose moves carefully when the evidence is weak.

The mechanism is simple: encode doubt into the map, then query the map when making decisions. The robot becomes conservative in uncertain places and confident only where the evidence is strong. This is faster because you look up a precomputed doubt score instead of computing confidence fresh from the image every step; it is safer because the doubt scores are based on multiple perturbations of the 3D map, giving more reliable estimates than a single-step guess.

stages.s: Perturb each Gaussian shape; measure output shift
Store geometric, semantic, appearance doubt at each blob
Query doubt map when choosing next move

math.h2: The reliability score for one blob
math.words: For each Gaussian blob, measure how much the rendered prediction changes when you nudge the blob's shape slightly. Store the average change as the blob's uncertainty score.
math.equation: uncertainty_i = sum_over_nudges( || f(G_i + delta) - f(G_i) ||^2 ) / num_nudges
symbols: the i-th Gaussian blob (position, scale, semantic label)
a small random perturbation to the blob parameters
the rendered observation (what the sensor sees when looking at blob i)
the squared difference (how far apart the two renderings are)
how much the blob's output shifts when jiggled

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Blob A: wall in clear light. Nudge position 3 pixels -> rendered image shifts by 0.2 units (small change). Nudge again -> shifts by 0.1 units. Average shift = 0.15. Uncertainty_A = 0.15 (low).
Blob B: wall in shadow. Nudge position 3 pixels -> rendered image shifts by 2.8 units (large change). Nudge again -> shifts by 2.6 units. Average shift = 2.7. Uncertainty_B = 2.7 (high).

Same nudge size, but shadow blob is unreliable because small changes in guessed position ripple into large changes in the rendered view. The map stores these scores, so the navigator knows which regions to trust.

math.note: Blobs with high uncertainty scores come from places where the robot's perception is fragile; the navigator uses these scores to avoid risky regions.

bars.h2: Comparison: naive agent vs. uncertainty-aware agent

charts.title: Naive agent (ignores doubt)
charts.note: The naive agent guesses confidently even when evidence is weak, so it fails when instructions are hard to interpret.

charts.title: This paper (uses uncertainty map)
charts.note: The uncertainty-aware agent is cautious in ambiguous regions, so it performs better overall.

items.html: If the perturbations do not capture the true sources of error (e.g. the robot is not actually sensitive to position changes, but IS sensitive to lighting), the uncertainty map will be misleading, and the robot will trust the wrong regions.

items.b: Uncertainty is correlated with hardness, not actually helpful
items.html: It is possible that high-uncertainty regions simply reflect hard tasks, not regions where the agent should be cautious. If so, the map might degrade performance instead of improving it, because the agent avoids difficult but solvable paths.

Computing uncertainty via perturbation (jiggling every blob many times and measuring the output shift) is expensive. If the perturbation budget is too low, the uncertainty estimates become noisy and unreliable.

items.b: Done right: validate on diverse environments
items.html: If the uncertainty estimates are accurate, and if the agent uses them conservatively (preferring certain regions), the agent performs better on ambiguous instructions because it avoids guessing in unclear areas, which is exactly where mistakes happen. It also does not get stuck on easy tasks because the uncertainty map is only cautious where evidence is actually weak.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulation with a 3D environment (a hallway with rooms), place the robot at a start location, and give it ambiguous instructions (e.g. 'go to the large room'—where there are two equally large rooms). Run the demo twice: first with a naive agent that ignores uncertainty, second with the uncertainty-aware agent. Plot the path each agent takes. On ambiguous instructions, the naive agent should wander and bump into walls; the uncertainty-aware agent should navigate via the high-confidence regions, arriving at the goal more reliably.
demo.closing: The demo must show: on ambiguous instructions, ignoring uncertainty fails, but measuring and using it succeeds.
